Launch page — revised messaging package (version 7; draft for review, not published)

Headline: “The AI manager for one-person companies.”

Subhead: “Somebody takes recurring work off your plate—so you can run the business without doing everything yourself.”

Primary audience:
Founders running a one-person company who need practical help carrying work through, not another generic business dashboard. The initial relaunch audience is one-person-company founders; lean SMEs are out of scope for this test unless separately specified.

Core message:
You built the business. Somebody helps run the work behind it. Delegate repeatable workflows to an AI manager that keeps tasks moving and gives you clear progress and outputs, so you can spend more time on the decisions only you can make.

What this addresses:
- Audience: names one-person-company founders instead of generic “businesses.”
- Outcome: explains the practical result—work is carried through and progress/outputs are returned—rather than relying on the category label “AI manager.”
- Pain: addresses the founder’s workload and the need to run the business without doing everything personally, rather than the generic “too many tools” assumption.
- Promise: positions Somebody as capacity expansion and delegated execution, not merely advice or another dashboard.

Supporting copy:
Somebody helps you move recurring work forward. Start with a workflow, delegate the repeatable steps, and get clear progress and outputs back. You stay responsible for the decisions that matter; Somebody helps carry the work between them.

Primary CTA:
“See how Somebody can run the work”

Rationale:
The current signal is low signup conversion and visitors do not recognise themselves. This revision explicitly identifies one-person-company founders, connects the product to their workload, and explains the practical outcome of delegated execution. It is intended to test whether clearer audience recognition and outcome language improve signup conversion.

Success criteria and test plan:
- Compare the revised page with the current page in a controlled comparison before publishing or promoting it broadly.
- Preregister audience, traffic source, sample size, test window, primary metric, and decision parameters before the test starts.
- Primary success criterion: higher signup conversion for the revised page than the current page, with the decision threshold set in the preregistration.
- Guardrail: no decline in audience recognition, measured by a predefined recognition question or equivalent instrument.
- Secondary diagnostic: CTA click-through rate.
- Do not declare a relaunch winner from directional results alone; record the sample, window, estimates, and uncertainty.

Relaunch decision:
Proceed to owner review and preregistration, then run the controlled comparison. Publish the revised message only if the preregistered primary conversion criterion is met and the audience-recognition guardrail is not breached. Otherwise retain the current page or revise the message and test again.

Material unresolved assumptions:
- The stated capabilities—delegating repeatable workflows, keeping tasks moving, and returning clear progress and outputs—must be verified against the product before publication.
- The exact audience definition, traffic mix, sample size, test window, recognition instrument, conversion threshold, and decision rule remain to be preregistered.
- It is not yet established that clearer one-person-company positioning will improve conversion; that is the purpose of the controlled comparison.
- No paid promotion is assumed; any paid spend requires an explicit application-approved provider path.

Status: review-only draft; not published.

history.content:
Launch page — current message
Headline: "Somebody: an AI manager for your business."
Subhead: "Automate your workflows with AI."
Status: launch not converting; visitors leave without signing up.
Assumed audience: generic "businesses".
Assumed pain point: "too many tools".

Messaging review — principal weaknesses (for review; not published)

1. Audience is too broad and does not identify the intended buyer.
The current headline says "your business" and the assumed audience is generic businesses, while the launch goal is to convert one-person-company founders. The available launch signal says visitors do not recognise themselves. Likely effect: weaker audience understanding and relevance, causing lower engagement and signup conversion.

2. The value proposition describes a category, not a finished outcome.
"AI manager" can be understood as another dashboard or advisor unless the copy explains that work is actually carried through. The current message does not state what Somebody owns, does, or returns. Likely effect: visitors may not understand the product's practical difference or reason to continue, reducing engagement and conversion.

3. The pain statement is generic and tool-oriented.
"Automate your workflows with AI" does not reflect the founder-language pattern of switching between selling, researching, following up, and doing the work. Generic workflow automation is broad and tool-like; concrete language about owning an outcome and finishing the job is easier to understand. Likely effect: weaker resonance and comprehension, with less motivation to sign up.

4. Accountability and capability expansion are missing.
The current copy does not communicate the stronger desired outcome: one accountable system that can notice missing capability, get what it needs, do the work, and return with a finished result. Likely effect: the product may be perceived as advice or automation tooling rather than an accountable operating partner, weakening differentiation and conversion.

Recommended messaging direction
Lead with the one-person-company founder outcome and accountability; then explain the make-versus-buy capability underneath. A review candidate is: "Stop switching between every job in your business." Follow with: "Somebody is an AI manager for one-person companies: it notices what is missing, gets the capability it needs, does the work, and comes back with a finished result."

Evidence reviewed
- Company record: launch/context — low signup conversion; visitors do not recognise themselves; relaunch goal is conversion among one-person-company founders.
- Company record: company/profile — Somebody is built for one-person companies and lean SMEs.
- Linked proprietary audience evidence: sim_result_0c12fbbf3b6576ccc6092a80 — founder pain language, interpretation of "AI manager," and preference for concrete accountable outcomes over generic workflow automation.

Review note
This is a bounded draft for internal review only. It has not been sent or published.

- Pain: addresses the founder’s workload and the need to run the business without doing everything personally, rather than the generic “too many tools” assumption.
- Promise: positions Somebody as capacity expansion and delegated execution, not merely advice or another dashboard.

Principal current messaging weaknesses and likely effects:
1. The headline leads with the category label “AI manager” rather than the founder’s concrete outcome. Audience-language evidence indicates that “AI manager” is often read as another dashboard or advisor unless the copy makes clear that work is actually carried through. Likely effect: weaker immediate understanding and engagement, with potential contribution to low signup conversion.
2. The message uses broad workflow language (“delegate repeatable workflows”) without making accountability and finished-job ownership sufficiently prominent. Audience-language evidence indicates that generic “automate your workflows” language feels broad and tool-like, while concrete language about owning an outcome and finishing the job is easier to understand. Likely effect: visitors may fail to see the practical difference from existing tools, reducing relevance and conversion.
3. The founder’s lived context is under-specified. Audience-language evidence describes the pain as switching between selling, researching, following up, and doing the work. The current copy refers generally to recurring work and doing everything yourself, but does not name that switching burden. Likely effect: weaker self-recognition and engagement among the intended audience.
4. The strongest desired outcome—one accountable system that can notice missing capability, get what it needs, do the work, and return with a finished result—is not stated explicitly. Likely effect: uncertainty about what Somebody actually does and lower confidence in the value proposition, which may depress signup conversion.

Evidence and limits:
- Company record: launch/context reports low signup conversion and that visitors do not recognise themselves (read observation ev_1790034236720_5eiwfo). This establishes the observed business problem, not a causal attribution to any single line of copy.
- Supplied audience-language evidence (resultEvidenceId sim_result_0c12fbbf3b6576ccc6092a80) supports the interpretation of the category-label, broad-language, lived-pain, and accountability weaknesses above. It is simulated proprietary social evidence, so the claims should be validated with live testing before publication.
- No claim here establishes that any particular weakness alone caused the conversion result.

Review recommendation:
Test a revised value proposition that leads with the founder outcome and accountability, then explains the make-versus-buy capability underneath. Verify capability claims, preregister the test parameters, and compare against the current page before publishing or promoting.

Success criteria:
- Primary metric: signup conversion.
- Supporting measures: audience recognition and engagement, using the owner’s preregistered definitions and test parameters.
- Decision rule: treat an inconclusive result as inconclusive; do not attribute causality without a controlled comparison and sufficient data.

Status:
Draft for review only. Nothing has been sent or published.

Launch page — revised messaging package (version 7; draft for review, not published)

Headline: “The AI manager for one-person companies.”

Subhead: “Somebody takes recurring work off your plate—so you can run the business without doing everything yourself.”

Primary audience:
Founders running a one-person company who need practical help carrying work through, not another generic business dashboard. The initial relaunch audience is one-person-company founders; lean SMEs are out of scope for this test unless separately specified.

Core message:
You built the business. Somebody helps run the work behind it. Delegate repeatable workflows to an AI manager that keeps tasks moving and gives you clear progress and outputs, so you can spend more time on the decisions only you can make.

What this addresses:
- Audience: names one-person-company founders instead of generic “businesses.”
- Outcome: explains the practical result—work is carried through and progress/outputs are returned—rather than relying on the category label “AI manager.”
- Pain: addresses the founder’s workload and the need to run the business without doing everything personally, rather than the generic “too many tools” assumption.
- Promise: positions Somebody as capacity expansion and delegated execution, not merely advice or another dashboard.

Supporting copy:
Somebody helps you move recurring work forward. Start with a workflow, delegate the repeatable steps, and get clear progress and outputs back. You stay responsible for the decisions that matter; Somebody helps carry the work between them.

Primary CTA:
“See how Somebody can run the work”

Rationale:
The current signal is low signup conversion and visitors do not recognise themselves. This revision explicitly identifies one-person-company founders, connects the product to their workload, and explains the practical outcome of delegated execution. It is intended to test whether clearer audience recognition and outcome language improve signup conversion.

Success criteria and test plan:
- Compare the revised page with the current page in a controlled comparison before publishing or promoting it broadly.
- Preregister audience, traffic source, sample size, test window, primary metric, and decision parameters before the test starts.
- Primary success criterion: higher signup conversion for the revised page than the current page, with the decision threshold set in the preregistration.
- Guardrail: no decline in audience recognition, measured by a predefined recognition question or equivalent instrument.
- Secondary diagnostic: CTA click-through rate.
- Do not declare a relaunch winner from directional results alone; record the sample, window, estimates, and uncertainty.

Relaunch decision:
Proceed to owner review and preregistration, then run the controlled comparison. Publish the revised message only if the preregistered primary conversion criterion is met and the audience-recognition guardrail is not breached. Otherwise retain the current page or revise the message and test again.

Material unresolved assumptions:
- The stated capabilities—delegating repeatable workflows, keeping tasks moving, and returning clear progress and outputs—must be verified against the product before publication.
- The exact audience definition, traffic mix, sample size, test window, recognition instrument, conversion threshold, and decision rule remain to be preregistered.
- It is not yet established that clearer one-person-company positioning will improve conversion; that is the purpose of the controlled comparison.
- No paid promotion is assumed; any paid spend requires an explicit application-approved provider path.

Status: review-only draft; not published.
